one_liner: Fork of Go's hash/crc32 adding an AVX-512 VPCLMULQDQ path that roughly doubles IEEE CRC32 throughput on inputs of 1 KB and up.
what_it_does: A copy of the Go standard library hash/crc32 package (rebased on Go 1.24 source in July 2025) with one extra amd64 kernel for the IEEE polynomial. The API is the stdlib one (Checksum, ChecksumIEEE, Update, New, NewIEEE, MakeTable, IEEE/Castagnoli/Koopman), so adoption is an import-path swap to github.com/klauspost/crc32. Output is bit-identical to hash/crc32; only the speed changes.
how_it_is_fast: It uses carry-less-multiply folding from Intel's 'Fast CRC Computation for Generic Polynomials Using PCLMULQDQ' paper, widened from 128-bit XMM to 512-bit ZMM registers. Each loop iteration folds 64 bytes with two VPCLMULQDQ ops and merges them with a three-way XOR in one VPTERNLOGD. The 512-bit accumulator is then split into four 128-bit lanes and handed to the existing SSE tail and Barrett reduction. Below 1024 bytes it falls back to the stdlib SSE4.1/PCLMULQDQ kernel, and to slicing-by-8 below 64 bytes.
when_to_use: Go services on Go 1.23-1.25 that compute IEEE CRC32 (gzip, zip, PNG, Ethernet-style checksums) over buffers of 1 KB or more on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VPCLMULQDQ
Checksumming large blobs in single calls (file chunks, network payloads, object-store parts), where the author measured 45-48 GB/s against about 20-22 GB/s on a Ryzen 9 9950X
When you want a pure-Go (no cgo) path that is bit-identical to hash/crc32, with the only change being the import line
when_not_to_use: You build with Go 1.26 or newer: the same AVX-512 IEEE code was merged into the standard library's hash/crc32 (golang/go commit 18dbe5b, present in go1.26.0, absent in go1.25.0), so this package adds nothing but a dependency

CRC32C (Castagnoli) or Koopman workloads: the Castagnoli AVX-512 kernel ships disabled (an 'if false' guard, with a comment saying it is not significantly faster even on Zen 5), so those polynomials run at stdlib speed
Short inputs or streaming with small Write calls: the AVX-512 path is chosen per call only when len(p) >= 1024, so 15 B-512 B checksums and sub-1 KB chunked writes see 1.00x
CPUs without AVX-512 (older x86, arm64, ppc64le, s390x, loong64): you get the stdlib-derived code paths and no speedup
Code that needs hash.Cloner: the Go 1.25+/1.26 stdlib digest has a Clone() method and this package's digest does not

integration.dependencies: golang.org/x/sys (v0.34.0, used for CPU feature detection via x/sys/cpu)
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.23 (go.mod declares go 1.23.0; CI tests 1.23.x and 1.24.x)
integration.platforms: any Go target. The AVX-512 speedup needs x86-64 with AVX512F, AVX512VL and AVX512 VPCLMULQDQ. Other targets use stdlib-derived assembly (amd64 SSE4.1/SSE4.2/PCLMULQDQ, arm64, ppc64le, s390x, loong64) or a generic Go fallback.
integration.thread_safety: Lazy table initialization is guarded by sync.OnceFunc and atomics, so Checksum/Update can be called concurrently. Each hash.Hash32 digest holds mutable state and, as in stdlib, should not be shared across goroutines; the README does not document this.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the README calls it a drop-in and the API and outputs match hash/crc32 for Go 1.23/1.24 code. However, crc32.Table is a distinct type, so tables cannot be shared with hash/crc32, and the Clone() method that stdlib digests gained in Go 1.25 is missing.

gotchas: The AVX-512 decision is made on each Update/Write call's length, not on the total stream length. A hash.Hash32 fed 512-byte chunks never uses the fast path, so batch writes into 1 KB+ slices.
The README warns that AVX-512 'may be slower to ramp up' for cold or short bursts, and says the published benchmarks, which run hot back-to-back loops, do not show this.
CI runs 'go test -tags=noasm', but no source file honors a noasm tag, so there is no build tag to force the portable path on amd64.
The 2025 rebase onto Go 1.24 source dropped the old gccgo/App Engine build constraints (earlier PRs #8 and #12). Non-gc toolchains are not tested.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this when you are in Go, cannot move to Go 1.26 yet, and want CRC32 with no cgo. crc-fast (Rust core with a C API) and corsix/fast-crc32 (C kernels) are the choice for peak GB/s or CRC32C outside Go, and crc32fast is the Rust-native option. Their multi-stream kernels go well beyond this package's single-accumulator AVX-512 loop.
verified_claims_summary: On an AMD Ryzen 9 9950X, go test -bench BenchmarkCRC32 (IEEE, 512 B-32 KB, aligned and offset-by-1 buffers) measured 45.6-48.6 GB/s for the AVX-512 path at 1-32 KB, against 19.9-21.9 GB/s for the stdlib-derived SSE4.1/PCLMULQDQ kernel it replaces (2.09x-2.35x), and 1.00x at 512 B and below. The Go toolchain version and flags are not stated. The author's upstream Go CL on the same CPU reported a similar 2.10x-2.44x.
status_note: The last commit and v1.3.0 tag are from 2025-07-22. The same author got the identical change into Go's hash/crc32 two days later (in Go 1.26), so this BSD-3-Clause module now mainly serves projects pinned to Go 1.23-1.25 and is effectively superseded rather than abandoned.
